rows.title: 3.0CL automatic transmission slips and fails — flush is forbidden, filter is not serviceable
rows.howToFix: If symptoms appear, immediately switch to ONLY Acura/Honda ATF (never Dextron substitute) and start a regular drain-and-refill schedule at every engine oil change interval (6 months). Do NOT power-flush — this transmission has effectively no serviceable filter and pressurized flushing forces debris through tight passages. If slipping has already started, a transmission specialist (not a quick-lube) needs to drop the pan to check for clutch material in the fluid. Once debris is visible, only a rebuild fixes it ($2,500-3,500). Replacements/rebuilds may need a fresh torque converter — the original is a known weak point. Add an aftermarket transmission cooler at rebuild time; the factory cooling is undersized.

rows.title: Ignition cylinder wear → shift interlock fails → rollaway risk (NHTSA recall 03V423000, 2003)
rows.howToFix: Check VIN at owners.acura.com/recalls or NHTSA recall lookup to confirm whether your specific car was included. If yes, schedule the free dealer fix — they replace the interlock assembly in about 30 min. If your dealer claims the recall is 'closed' or 'no longer covered,' escalate to American Honda Customer Service (800-382-2238) — safety recalls have no expiration date under federal law (49 CFR §573.6). If you can't get to a dealer, ALWAYS verify the shifter is fully in Park and the parking brake is set before removing the key. This is not a workaround — it's a discipline check that protects you while you arrange the free repair.

rows.title: 8-Speed DCT Shudder and Low-Speed Jerking
rows.howToFix: Update the DCT software to the latest Acura calibration which improves low-speed clutch engagement. Perform a DCT fluid change with genuine Honda DCTF. In severe cases, the clutch pack assembly needs replacement. Acura extended warranty coverage on the DCT to 7 years/100,000 miles due to widespread complaints.

rows.title: Infotainment System Lag and Unresponsive Touchscreen
rows.howToFix: Update infotainment firmware to the latest available version. Perform a factory reset to clear cached data. Reduce the number of paired Bluetooth devices to three or fewer. If the touchscreen digitizer has failed, the lower screen unit needs replacement.

rows.title: Engine motor mounts crack and collapse — drivetrain vibration + clunk on shifts
rows.howToFix: Replace mounts one at a time as they fail, not all four preemptively (the front and side mounts can last 200k+). Diagnose by having a helper rev the engine in neutral while you look — a healthy mount holds the engine still; a dead one lets the engine rock 1-2 inches. Common pattern: rear mount + passenger-side mount are the first two to need replacement, and both are visible from above without lifting. Aftermarket options range from cheap rubber ($30 each) to Energy Suspension polyurethane ($60-100, transmits more vibration but lasts forever) to Innovative Mounts billet ($100-200, used for tracked cars). For a daily-driver Integra, OEM Honda rubber or Cardone is the right balance. Total cost replacing rear + side: $80-300 in parts, 2-3 hours of labor.

rows.title: Outer CV joint boot tears leading to joint failure and clicking
rows.howToFix:
If the boot has just torn and no elements got into the joint, regreasing and rebooting can work — a $10 boot kit vs. a $60 replacement axle is the tradeoff.
 
Reman axles run around $50 each and boot kits about $25 — AutoZone and similar carry both for the 1992 Integra 1.8L DOHC.
 
Pack outer CV joint boot with molybdenum disulfide grease, lube the spider and inside bore of rollers, ensure rollers are aligned with marks made at disassembly and install with the high side of rollers facing outward.
 Use new boot clamps (low-profile metal bands included in kit). Most owners simply swap the full reman half-shaft for under $100/side — quicker than rebooting. Always replace the axle nut and use a new transaxle retaining ring.

rows.title: Distributor internal shaft seal fails, oil leaks into cap and causes misfires + stalling
rows.howToFix: Replace the complete distributor. OEM Honda distributors are pricey ($350-500+) but reliable; aftermarket units from Cardone, A1 Cardone, or Spectra Premium are $80-150 and work fine for non-track use. While the distributor is out, also replace the cap, rotor, and ignition wires — they're cheap and replacing them at the same time saves a labor cycle. After install, time the engine to factory spec (16°±2° BTDC at idle with timing-adjust connector unplugged). Do NOT just clean the cap and call it done — the oil keeps coming and you'll be back in 6 weeks. If you're keeping the car long-term, the Honda OEM distributor outlasts aftermarket 2:1.

rows.title: Ignitor / ignition control module inside the distributor fails — intermittent or no-start
rows.howToFix: Test the ignitor before replacing — a multimeter check at the coil primary terminals while cranking will confirm whether the module is sending pulse to the coil. If no pulse: replace. OEM Honda module $80-150, aftermarket (Beck Arnley, Delphi) $30-80. The module sits inside the distributor cap; replacement requires removing the cap and rotor, unscrewing 2 mounting screws, and transferring the heat sink if present (Civic/Integra units may require heat sink #30121-PM5-A02 for correct fitment). Inspect the inside of the distributor cap and rotor for moisture or corrosion while you're in there — a cracked cap allows water in and causes premature module failure on the replacement. Replace cap + rotor at the same time as a preventive measure.

Inspect the inside of the distributor cap and rotor for moisture or corrosion while you're in there — a cracked cap allows water in and causes premature module failure on the replacement.

rows.title: Motorized passive shoulder belt sticks on track or fails to move
rows.howToFix:
The seat-belt fuses are under the hood on the passenger-side shock tower — the fuse-box cover labels them; pull and inspect the passive motor L and R fuses (30A each) first.
 
Manually unstick the belt by locating the rod with a hex-head fitting on the motor, then use a screwdriver/Allen key to drive the seat-belt motor manually to the rear position before closing the door.
 
American Acura/Honda has a policy of offering a lifetime warranty on the functional components of their seat belts — as long as the vehicle is an American-market car, has not been in a collision, and the belt assembly has not been modified, American Acura will fix it at their cost; if the dealer refuses, phone Acura Client Relations at (800) 382-2238.
 Note that Honda Canada does not honor this policy.

diagnosticDispositions.excerpt: pull and inspect the passive motor L and R fuses (30A each) first.

rows.title: Passenger-side cowl seal leak floods blower motor and floor pan
rows.howToFix:
Order eight of Honda part number 91608-SJ6-003 (the clear grommet/seal pieces) from a Honda or Acura dealer — they are inexpensive at roughly $2.50 each.
 Remove the wiper arms (14mm) and the black plastic cowl, clear out all leaf debris from the drainage channels, then replace the old foam strip with new urethane weatherstripping and reinstall with the new grommets. 
Remove the wipers, pop the 7-8 pins, undo the pins along the perimeter under the hood, clean out the drainage paths, scrape out the old weather stripping, and replace with 1/4" wide, 1/2" thick urethane weather stripping for a permanent fix.
 If the blower motor or resistor has already corroded, replace those at the same time.

rows.title: PGM-FI main relay solder joint cracks cause hot-weather no-start
rows.howToFix:
Replacing the main relay is one of the easiest repairs on the Integra; it is located under the driver's-side dash, near the hood release lever and to the right of the parking brake pedal — unbolt the mounting bracket (10mm), unplug the harness, and plug in the new relay.
 
Use a quality replacement — the DA-chassis OEM part number is typically 39400-PM6-003 (verify with your VIN at an Acura dealer or parts store, as several supersessions exist). Reputable aftermarket cross-references include Standard Motor Products RY-passenger-style relays, Beck/Arnley, and Denso. Expect to pay $25-$80 for the part and avoid the cheapest generic relays — reliability matters.
 
Resoldering the cracked joints on the existing relay's circuit board has been done successfully by many owners, but requires skill with a soldering iron and may not be permanent — a new aftermarket relay is the more reliable repair.

rows.title: Rear quarter panel and rocker panel rust-through behind wheel arch protectors
rows.howToFix:
All G2 Integras came with rear wheel arch protectors — pull them off as preventive maintenance; Acura wanted around $40-$50 each for them new.
 For early rust, cut out affected metal with at least one inch of clean margin, treat the inner frame with a rust converter such as POR-15, and weld in patch panels (92-95 Civic patch panels can be modified to fit). 
Proper repair is to replace the complete rear quarter — body shop estimates run around $4000 for both sides with paint; DIY gutting/stripping can drop it closer to $2000-$3500.
 Aftermarket wheel arch and quarter patch panels are available from Mill Supply and other restoration vendors.
rows.dispositionReason: The remedy is a service, tool, consumable, or fluid procedure rather than a repair part.

rows.title: Rear wheel bearing hum from press-in hub assembly
rows.howToFix:
This is an advanced DIY job. Some owners replace the rear as a complete pre-pressed hub assembly (commonly $80-$120 from aftermarket suppliers), which avoids press work; others source just the bearing/race and press it into the spindle/knuckle using a hydraulic shop press (or have a machine shop do it). Front bearings on the DA always require pressing into the knuckle.
 Quality replacement brands include SKF, Timken, FAG, Koyo and NSK (the latter two are often OEM suppliers to Honda).
 Rear bearings are a bit more expensive but easier to access than the fronts.
 Budget $40-$120 per bearing/assembly plus press/labor; total shop cost typically $200-$450 per corner.

rows.title: 4-speed automatic: shift solenoid failure causes D4 light flash, missed shifts, and limp mode
rows.howToFix:
Drain-and-fill with Honda ATF-Z1/DW-1 (NEVER use generic Dexron — it will destroy the clutches). 
The transmission fluid in the Integra 4AT's are supposed to be changed every 3 years/36,000 mi. It can cook and wear out just like the oil in your engine.
 Pull codes with a Honda jumper or scan tool; the lock-up and shift solenoids are external, three-bolt parts accessible from the engine bay and often just need cleaning. 
A screwed up lock-up solenoid will give you a general CEL #70 (Automatic Transaxle); the solenoid is totally accessible from the engine bay and costs less than $200 to replace. It's held in place by three bolts.

rows.title: Internal distributor failure causing stalling, no-start, and misfires
rows.howToFix:
Pull DTCs first — codes P1381 (cylinder position sensor) and Code 22 commonly originate inside the distributor. 
P1381 is the cylinder position sensor code, located inside the distributor.
 Replace the complete OEM distributor assembly (avoid cheap aftermarket — many fail within months). OBD1 (94-95) and OBD2 (96-99) distributors are not interchangeable. 
It is worth noting that the distributor plugs are different for each obd generation. So the obd1, and obd2 have different harness plugs.
 Budget $250-550 for a quality unit installed.

rows.title: Ignition switch contact pitting causes engine to die when key released
rows.howToFix:
Replace the ignition switch electrical portion (not the cylinder/lock) — it unbolts from the back of the steering column lock housing with two screws. OEM Honda part is the most reliable choice. 
The issue is starting the car and it dies as soon as you let go of the key. After research, it became obvious it was an ignition switch issue.
 Check the under-hood main fuse and the ignition fuses before condemning the switch. Budget $50-150 for parts and 1 hour labor.

rows.title: Rear lower control arm bolts seize and shear inside bushing sleeves
rows.howToFix:
Soak bolts with penetrating fluid (PB Blaster/Kroil) for days before attempting removal; heat the bushing sleeve with a torch. If the bolt shears, the only fix is to cut the bushing out and drill/punch the remaining sleeve from the subframe ear. 
When you are down there and replacing rusted bolts, if they are rusted on bad enough you might have to break the welded nut they go into on the front side of the subframe and trailing arms. You can get matching sized nuts and washers.
 Replace with OEM Honda bolts (M10x1.25, ~$4-9 each from the dealer). 
Diameter = 10mm, Pitch = 1.25.

rows.title: Timing belt failure on interference B18 engine bends valves
rows.howToFix:
Replace the complete timing belt kit: belt, tensioner, tensioner spring, water pump, cam and crank seals, and balance shaft belt where applicable.
Non-VTEC LS (B18B1) timing belt part numbers are 14400-P7J-004 or 14400-PR4-A01, paired with the 19-tooth water pump 19200-P75-003 / 19200-PT5-000 / 19200-PT5-003. The VTEC GSR (B18C1) uses timing belt 14400-P72-004 / 14400-P72-014 paired with a 22-tooth water pump.
Do NOT mix LS and GSR water pumps — the tooth counts differ (19T vs 22T) and the belts are different lengths.
Professional cost for preventive replacement: approximately $350-600. Post-failure repair (valve job / head rebuild) can reach $2,000-3,000+.

rows.title: Turbo Heat Soak and Power Loss in Hot Weather
rows.howToFix: Allow 2-3 minutes of gentle driving between spirited runs to cool the intake charge. Ensure the intercooler fins are clean and unobstructed by debris. Aftermarket intercooler upgrades significantly reduce heat soak on the 1.5T. The Type S 2.0T is less affected due to its larger factory intercooler but still benefits from airflow improvements.

rows.title: Timing belt must be replaced at 90,000 mi / 72 months — interference engine eats valves if it snaps
rows.howToFix: Replace the timing belt every 90,000 miles OR 72 months — and treat the 72-month limit as the binding one on cars over 15 years old, regardless of mileage. The job is a full front-of-engine teardown: remove crank pulley, front cover, all accessory belts. While you're in there, ALWAYS replace the water pump, timing belt tensioner, all front seals (crank, cam, balance shaft), and idler pulley as a kit — the labor to replace any one of them later is 90% of the timing belt labor. Use OEM Mitsuboshi/Bando belts from Acura or top-tier aftermarket (Aisin, Gates Powergrip). Expect $600-1,000 in parts and $500-900 in labor at an independent. Skip the dealer ($1,500-2,000+) unless they're running a special.

rows.title: Fan control unit circuit board (under passenger area) has defective solder — intermittent A/C, eventual no-compressor (Acura TSB 95-020)

Re-flow the joints with a soldering iron and a small amount of fresh solder. Total cost: $0 in parts, 1 hour of labor. Replacement units are scarce and expensive ($150-300 used) so the solder-repair is the standard fix. Acura specialists and Honda forums have documented the exact joints — search 'Acura Legend fan control unit solder' for board photos showing the failure points.

rows.title: ALB/ABS modulator pump times out and pressure sensor fails on NA1 NSX (1991-1999)
rows.howToFix: Three repair paths, from cheap to expensive. (1) DIY O-ring rebuild with the SOS or egmCarTech kit ($105-200), which replaces the brake-fluid-resistant O-rings inside the modulator; the kit includes a bleeder T-wrench and 28-piece O-ring set. (2) Professional rebuild by a specialist (AutoECU, ScienceofSpeed, etc.) for around $795 — they pull the unit, replace O-rings and the pump motor brushes if worn. (3) Dealer full-assembly replacement at $2,100-2,600. There is also a documented upgrade path to swap the 1991-1999 NA1 modulator for the 2000-2005 NA2 unit using the SOS conversion kit, which simplifies the system and improves long-term reliability. Before any repair, check that the failure isn't simply rodent damage to the pump motor wires under the car — a blown ALB fuse from chewed wires presents the same way and costs $10 to fix.

rows.title: Climate control unit display pixel fade and dead buttons (1991-1999 NA1)
rows.howToFix: Mail-in CCU repair from an NSX specialist is the standard fix. ScienceofSpeed, AutoTechRescue, SpeedoFix, NSXe-repair, and ModuleRepairPro all offer rebuild service for around $150-300 with 1-3 day turnaround. Removal is a 20-30 minute job at home — pop the armrest, shift knob, ashtray, and center console trim, then four screws hold the CCU. Reinstallation requires no programming or coding. Avoid full Acura CCU replacement: even when available, the part is over $1,000 and the rebuilt original works identically. Common rebuild scope: LCD module, all rubber button pads, electrolytic capacitors C1/C2/C3 on the main board, and reflow on heat-stressed solder joints.

rows.title: Snap-ring transmission failure on 1991-1992 NSX (serial range J4A4-1003542 to J4A4-1005978)
rows.howToFix: Two paths: (1) Acura dealer transmission replacement runs about $7,000-7,500 in parts and labor — this swaps the entire assembly. (2) An NSX specialist (ScienceofSpeed, NSX Modified, etc.) can rebuild the existing transmission and replace the upper case half for around $2,500-4,675 depending on shop and gear set choice, saving $3,000-4,500 vs dealer. Preventive repair before failure (replacing the upper case while gears are still intact) is about 10 hours labor + $700 parts. If the snap ring has already shattered, debris in the gear oil mandates a full teardown — do not just refill and drive. Honda's original goodwill program tapered off sharply in 1999, so post-2000 repairs are owner-paid.

rows.title: Targa roof gaskets harden, wind noise increases and water leaks under heavy rain
rows.howToFix: Two stages. PREVENTIVE: clean the gaskets monthly with isopropyl alcohol, then apply Honda Shin-Etsu silicone grease (P/N 08798-9013) — this is the same grease used on the door weatherstripping and prevents drying-out. A small tube ($15-25) lasts years. If gaskets are already cracked or compression-set, REPLACE: OEM Honda Targa seals run $300-500 for the set. Use the exact butyl tape (0.5mm) and EPT sealer (3.0mm) called out in the service manual, plus sealant #08712-0004. Most NSX owners use an NSX specialist (ScienceofSpeed, Driving Ambition, NSX Modified) for the install — $400-700 in labor — rather than DIY, because the alignment determines water-tightness and a mis-bedded seal leaks worse than the old one.

Replace the receiver/drier and expansion valve at the same time. Evacuate and recharge the system with the correct amount of R-134a refrigerant. Inspect the serpentine belt for damage from the seized clutch.

rows.title: Distributor shaft seal leaks oil into cap, causes misfires (P0300-P0304) on 3.5L C35A
rows.howToFix: There is no replaceable seal inside the distributor — the seal is between the rotating shaft and the bearing inside the cast housing. The only fix is replacing the whole distributor assembly. OEM Honda runs $400-700; Cardone remanufactured runs $150-250. While the distributor is out, also replace the distributor cap, rotor, and ignition wires — they're cheap and you're already at the parts. Inspect the cap and rotor on the old unit for oil contamination to confirm distributor was the source. If you also see leaks elsewhere (figure-8 cooler seal, oil filter housing), address those at the same time — they share access path. Total job: 2-3 hours independent shop.

Dealer: $2,000-2,800. Never use a generic 'timing belt only' service — replacing the belt without the water pump or tensioner is a guarantee of a second teardown within 30,000 miles.

If noise persists after fluid change, the rear differential unit needs rebuilding with new clutch packs. Replace the electromagnetic actuators if they are not engaging properly. Regular fluid changes every 30,000 miles prevent premature clutch pack wear.

rows.title: AC Compressor Clutch Bearing Failure

rows.title: Consumer Reports rated the 1996 SLX 'Not Acceptable' for rollover risk in low-speed turns
rows.howToFix: There is no mechanical fix because there's no mechanical defect — the Consumer Reports finding was a stability characteristic, not a failed part. Buyers and owners should: (1) know the vehicle's center of gravity is high; avoid emergency lane-change maneuvers above 35 mph if possible. (2) Keep the suspension and tires in spec — worn shocks and underinflated tires make rollover more likely on any tall SUV. (3) Use the OEM-spec tire size; oversized off-road tires raise the center of gravity further. (4) Modern stability control didn't exist on the SLX — drive accordingly. Used-buyer tip: the SLX/Trooper market is depressed permanently because of this story, which makes well-maintained examples a relative bargain — but go in eyes-open about the handling envelope.

rows.title: Rear differential whine + transfer case (BW4422) failures inherited from Isuzu Trooper platform
rows.howToFix: REAR DIFF: If whine is noticed early, change the gear oil to fresh 80W-90 GL-5 and run a friction modifier. This will not stop existing wear but can slow it. Once whine is pronounced, the only durable fix is a remanufactured rear axle assembly ($800-1,400) or a rebuild of the existing ring and pinion ($1,200-2,000 at a specialist). TRANSFER CASE: Verify the manufacturer-spec fluid is being used — DO NOT default to motor oil or ATF without confirming. Check fluid level every oil change. If the case is whining or has external leaks, source the correct Borg-Warner rebuild kit by part number from your vehicle's exact model year + transmission combination — multiple BW transfer case variants were used across SLX/Trooper years and the parts are NOT interchangeable.

rows.title: 1999 3.2TL 5-speed auto was the start of the famous Acura V6 transmission failures
rows.howToFix: If you own a 1999 TL with the 5AT and it's slipping, flaring on shifts, or showing harsh 1-2 / 2-3 changes: STOP driving aggressively immediately. The damage compounds quickly. Get a transmission specialist (not a dealer) to drop the pan and check for clutch material in the fluid. If found, the only durable fix is a rebuilt transmission ($2,500-4,000) — not a fluid change, not a solenoid swap. The original Honda warranty extension to 7/100k expired in 2006, so out-of-pocket cost is now on the owner. Many owners install an aftermarket transmission cooler with the rebuild — the original spec is undersized for the load and contributed to the failure pattern. Avoid 'flush' services — pressurized flushes on a worn transmission accelerate failure by dislodging clutch debris.
